narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 63.8% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was denied.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. First, your family income bracket of Middle had the strongest influence and pushed the prediction toward failure. Although middle-income students make up about 35% of accepted applicants, this bracket was associated with a higher risk of not passing the bar compared with students from higher-income families.

Second, your first-year law school grades placed you in the 5th decile, noticeably below the average of 6th decile among accepted students. This weaker early performance was the second most important reason the model leaned toward predicting failure.

Third, your LSAT score of 39 was actually slightly above the average of 37 for accepted students and worked in your favor, gently pulling the prediction toward passing. However, this positive effect was not strong enough to overcome the combined impact of your family income bracket and first-year grades.

Your later grades, undergraduate GPA, full-time status, gender, and race played only minor roles and were not deciding factors.

To improve your chances, focus on strengthening your academic record in the remaining years of law school and consider resources or support programs that have helped middle-income students raise their bar passage rates. Reapply once you have demonstrated clearer progress in those key areas.
